$$\begin{aligned} y' &= e^{-2x} + -2(1 + x)e^{-2x} \\ &= e^{-2x}\left(1 - 2(1 + x)\right) \\ &= e^{-2x}(-1 - 2x) \\ y' &= -e^{-2x}(1 + 2x) \end{aligned}$$

Let $y' = 0$: $0 = -e^{-2x}(1 + 2x)$

$\therefore 0 = -e^{-2x}$ (no solutions) and $0 = 1 + 2x$, so $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, $y = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-2 \times -\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{e}{2}$

$\therefore \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$ is a stationary point.

Testing:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & -1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ \hline y' & e^2 & 0 & -1 \\ & / & - & \backslash \end{array}$$

$\therefore$ Maximum turning point at $\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{e}{2}\right)$

$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} &= 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) &= \dfrac{t}{10} \\ \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) &= \dfrac{t}{10} \\ 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) &= t \\ t &= 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$I = \dfrac{ky}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$

$u = ky$, $u' = k$, $v = \left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}$, $v' = 3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dy} &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} - ky \times 3y\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\left(\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left[\left(y^2 + a^2\right) - 3y^2\right]}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{k\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^3} \\ \dfrac{dI}{dy} &= \dfrac{k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right)}{\left(y^2 + a^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \end{aligned}$$

Let $\dfrac{dI}{dy} = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= k\left(a^2 - 2y^2\right) \\ 0 &= a^2 - 2y^2 \\ 2y^2 &= a^2 \\ y^2 &= \dfrac{a^2}{2} \\ y &= \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \text{as } y > 0 \end{aligned}$$

Test:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} y & 0 & \frac{a}{\sqrt{2}} & a \\ \hline \frac{dI}{dy} & \frac{k}{a^3} & 0 & \frac{-ka^2}{\left(2a^2\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}} \\ & / & - & \backslash \end{array}$$

$\therefore$ Maximum value at $y = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ m
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: Correct derivative, correctly finding $y$, testing for maximum; 2: Two of the above (or 1 error); 1: One of the above
